caption:
Everybody chases the hind end. The front end starts the movement.

When a horse short-strides up front, riders assume it's a shoulder, a tendon, or an old injury. Sometimes it is. But a surprising number of cases Dr. Leo sees in North Texas trace back to restriction at the withers and the first few ribs — the area that controls how far forward that front leg reaches.

Three things that point there before you ever call the vet:
— One shoulder consistently lands shorter, but no heat, no swelling
— Head carriage shifts slightly to one side at the lope
— She resists collection or feels "sticky" picking up one rein

None of those are dramatic. None of them show up on an X-ray. But they all affect your run.
